{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-tn","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"1c7df6ef160b98dbc8bbb0f6bed63f076a26407643240c857e11389844ea88e0","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-tn-class-d:lineage:28","source_registry_sha256":"8b0b6a068a0aa720d419171b5007a2610ed6c5012eeff522b57713cf9226eb71","source_liveness_sha256":"d27b9a94f03ec29d960b8eea38966606a7d3fdb703ad30b19ecd93f9bc70d0c7"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C2"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C2","chunk_id":"C2.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Sign, signal and marking confusables and continuation details","heading":"C2 — Confusable pairs and knowledge-graph hints: turn versus curve signs, stop-ahead and yield-ahead warnings, work zone devices and flaggers, guide and route signs, reference markers, pedestrian and lane signals, HOV lanes and other markings","learner_facing":false,"markdown":"## C2 — Confusable pairs and knowledge-graph hints: turn versus curve signs, stop-ahead and yield-ahead warnings, work zone devices and flaggers, guide and route signs, reference markers, pedestrian and lane signals, HOV lanes and other markings
Confusable pairs and continuation facts for traffic control devices, from the manual's text only; each block ties to one manual page, and hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec07-R01 | anchor: A01
Black is used for regulatory signs and for the message on white, yellow and orange signs, while white also serves as the lettering on brown, green, blue, black and red signs. [A01]
Why it matters: group sign colors; confusable background color versus legend color.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0049]

FACT_ID: sec07-R02 | anchor: A01
Wherever the manual says a sign is white, that includes silver reflective coating or material that reflects white light. [A01]
Why it matters: group sign colors; difficulty low.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0049]

FACT_ID: sec07-R03 | anchor: A02
Temporary traffic control zones let traffic move safely past an incident while protecting drivers, responders and equipment, and may use message signs, warning lights, flags, barricades and cones. [A02]
Why it matters: group incident zones; links fluorescent pink.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec07-R04 | anchor: A02
A diamond warning sign drawn as a small road map shows the kind of intersection ahead, such as a crossroad. [A02]
Why it matters: group warning signs; difficulty low.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec07-R05 | anchor: A03
Some lane control signs require trucks to use certain lanes or tell each lane to go straight or turn left, and they are sometimes mounted overhead. [A03]
Why it matters: group lane signs; difficulty low.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec07-R06 | anchor: A03
A High Occupancy Vehicle sign marks lanes reserved for buses and vehicles carrying at least the number of people shown. [A03]
Why it matters: group lane signs; links HOV markings.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec07-R07 | anchor: A04
The turn sign marks a turn with a recommended speed of 30 mph or less, while the curve sign marks curves rated between 30 and 55 mph. [A04]
Why it matters: group warning signs; confusable turn sign versus curve sign.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec07-R08 | anchor: A04
A reverse turn sign marks two turns in opposite directions less than 600 feet apart. [A04]
Why it matters: group warning signs; difficulty medium.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec07-R09 | anchor: A04
A small advisory speed plate under a warning sign gives the recommended top safe speed for that hazard. [A04]
Why it matters: group warning signs; difficulty low.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec07-R10 | anchor: A04
The falling rocks sign warns of rocks lying on the road rather than rocks falling on you, so watch the pavement, not the hillside. [A04]
Why it matters: group warning signs; misconception rocks from above.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec07-R11 | anchor: A04
Stop-ahead and yield-ahead signs warn of a stop or yield sign you cannot yet see, and you should begin slowing when you pass them; a traffic-light symbol version warns of a signal ahead. [A04]
Why it matters: group warning signs; confusable stop ahead versus yield ahead versus signal ahead.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec07-R12 | anchor: A04
At a lane-ends sign, signal and merge into the remaining lane, and at a merging-traffic sign, check behind you and move over if you can to give merging drivers room. [A04]
Why it matters: group warning signs; confusable lane ends versus merging traffic.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec07-R13 | anchor: A04
A narrow bridge sign warns that the bridge may force passing cars to slow down. [A04]
Why it matters: group warning signs; difficulty low.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec07-R14 | anchor: A05
A low clearance sign gives the height from the road surface to the bottom of the bridge or overpass ahead. [A05]
Why it matters: group warning signs; difficulty low.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec07-R15 | anchor: A05
A T-intersection sign means you must turn right or left ahead and be prepared to yield, while chevron signs emphasize a sharp change in direction. [A05]
Why it matters: group warning signs; confusable T-intersection versus chevron.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec07-R16 | anchor: A05
Work zone signs are usually orange diamonds or rectangles with black letters or symbols, warning of workers, lower speeds, detours, slow equipment and lane closures. [A05]
Why it matters: group work zones; difficulty low.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec07-R17 | anchor: A05
In a work area you must obey a person directing traffic with a sign or flag. [A05]
Why it matters: group work zones; difficulty low.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec07-R18 | anchor: A05
A flashing arrow panel warns of a lane closure, and you must start merging into the open lane well before reaching it. [A05]
Why it matters: group work zones; difficulty medium.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec07-R19 | anchor: A05
Flaggers usually hold a paddle reading stop on one side and slow on the other, switching to red flags in emergencies, and the stop and proceed hand motions are the same either way. [A05]
Why it matters: group work zones; confusable paddle versus flag.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec07-R20 | anchor: A05
Among barricades, panels, barriers, drums and cones, keep to the middle of your lane at the posted speed, and do not change lanes until you are fully past the work zone. [A05]
Why it matters: group work zones; difficulty medium.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec07-R21 | anchor: A05
Officers, flaggers and other workers directing traffic wear fluorescent yellow-green, along with fluorescent orange for workers, so drivers can see them in poor light and bad weather. [A05]
Why it matters: group work zones; difficulty low.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec07-R22 | anchor: A06
The slow-moving vehicle emblem is a fluorescent orange triangle, highly visible by day, seen on farm tractors, construction equipment and horse-drawn vehicles, and it glows in headlights at night. [A06]
Why it matters: group special signs; difficulty low.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec07-R23 | anchor: A06
Object markers flag things just off the road edge, such as bridge ends and underpass supports. [A06]
Why it matters: group special signs; difficulty low.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec07-R24 | anchor: A06
A U.S. route sign shows black numbers on a white shield set on a black background, and a U.S. route continues into other states. [A06]
Why it matters: group route signs; confusable U.S. route versus state route.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec07-R25 | anchor: A06
Blue and red interstate route markers identify the national system of interstate and defense highways. [A06]
Why it matters: group route signs; difficulty low.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec07-R26 | anchor: A06
On interstate guide signs the arrows point to the lane you need to enter or leave the highway, and when a guide sign carries the must-exit marking, every vehicle in the lanes under those arrows must exit. [A06]
Why it matters: group guide signs; difficulty medium.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec07-R27 | anchor: A06
Parking spaces with the blue handicap symbol are reserved for vehicles with disabled veteran or handicapped plates or a special decal, and others may not use them. [A06]
Why it matters: group service signs; difficulty low.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec07-R28 | anchor: A07
Interstate reference markers stand every 1,000 feet on busy stretches in Nashville, Knoxville, Memphis, Jackson and Chattanooga, showing route, direction and log mile in tenths so callers can give their exact location. [A07]
Why it matters: group reference markers; difficulty medium.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec07-R29 | anchor: A07
Drivers who rush a yellow light risk colliding with cross-street drivers who jump the green early. [A07]
Why it matters: group signals; confusable beating the yellow versus jumping the green.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec07-R30 | anchor: A07
Do not pull into a busy intersection to turn until your path is clear, or you may be stranded inside it. [A07]
Why it matters: group signals; difficulty low.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec07-R31 | anchor: A08
A pedestrian who has started across on WALK should finish crossing as quickly as possible before DON'T WALK appears, and some signals need a push button to show WALK. [A08]
Why it matters: group pedestrian signals; difficulty low.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec07-R32 | anchor: A08
Lane control signals over each lane are mostly used where traffic direction changes by time of day, and they also show whether toll plaza lanes are open. [A08]
Why it matters: group lane signals; difficulty medium.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec07-R33 | anchor: A08
Tennessee's signs and markings follow the federal Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices, so drivers may see both old and new designs during updates. [A08]
Why it matters: group standards; difficulty low.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec07-R34 | anchor: A08
Yellow lines also outline hazards along the travel path, such as bridge supports. [A08]
Why it matters: group markings; difficulty low.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec07-R35 | anchor: A09
HOV lanes are marked by a diamond in the center of the lane or set apart by a barrier, and signs give the minimum passengers and the hours the limit applies. [A09]
Why it matters: group markings; links HOV signs.
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec07-R36 | anchor: A09
Double or triple pavement arrows allow more than one movement, while a single arrow allows only the one direction shown. [A09]
Why it matters: group markings; confusable single versus double arrows.
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec07-R37 | anchor: A09
A white crossbuck with the letters RR painted on the pavement warns of many railroad crossings ahead. [A09]
Why it matters: group markings; links railroad signs.
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0057]
